title: Malaysia and Singapore
hook: long-settled Sikh communities with old gurdwaras

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pakistan's Sikhs, and your line was across the border. Did you send a friendly word over a line? Today, roots that go down in warm, wet ground far from Punjab. Day one thousand thirty-one.

Afternoon rain hammers a tin roof. Ceiling fans turn slowly over a hall of people sitting cross-legged on white sheets. A harmonium and a tabla carry a hymn over the noise of the storm. Outside, frangipani trees drip, and a scooter splashes past. In the kitchen, rotis sit beside rice, because the cooks long ago learned what grows well here. This is a gurdwara in Penang, or Kuala Lumpur, or Singapore, and the families in the hall don't think of it as a new arrival. Their grandparents prayed here. Today is about Sikh roots that have had a long time to grow.
screen: `RAIN ON A TIN ROOF.` → `A HYMN OVER THE STORM.` → `THEIR GRANDPARENTS PRAYED HERE.`

segments.voice: First, the arrival. Community histories tell of Sikh men who came to Malaya and Singapore in the days of British rule, to serve in the police and as guards and watchmen, and of others who came to trade or to farm cattle. In time, wives and children followed, and a scattering of workers became a sangat. Second, the gurdwara. Community histories tell how, once a few families had settled, a place for the Guru soon followed. Some of those gurdwaras still stand, rebuilt and enlarged, with old photographs on the walls of men in turbans and uniforms. The gurdwara became the place for langar, for Punjabi classes, for weddings and for help finding work. Third, the roots. Families here now count generations born in the tropics. Children grow up speaking English and the languages around them, and learning Punjabi in the gurdwara so they can read the Guru's words. The weather changed, the food changed a little, the language around them changed. The hymns didn't. Fourth, the line underneath it. In a hymn by Guru Ram Das, at Ang 450 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru says that wherever the True Guru goes and sits, that place becomes beautiful. Some Sikhs hear in that a reason why no land is too far: where the Guru is seated and the sangat gathers, the place is made right. That is today's line: old roots abroad. A tree that grew where it was planted.
screen: `POLICE, GUARDS, TRADERS, FAMILIES.` · `FIRST, A PLACE FOR THE GURU.` · `GENERATIONS BORN IN THE TROPICS.` · `ANG 450: WHERE THE GURU SITS.` · then, large: `OLD ROOTS ABROAD.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in a gurdwara in the tropics. Sit, and let your breath slow. Hear, if you can, rain on a tin roof. Feel the fans moving warm air. See the white sheets, the canopy, the families in rows, the old photographs on the wall. Breathe in the smell of the kitchen. Breathe out, and let the sound of the hymn carry over the storm. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, the way the people in that hall might. If you don't, simply sit in the picture until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Malaysia and Singapore. Long-settled Sikh communities whose old gurdwaras have held generations of families far from Punjab. Today's word.

Your line: old roots abroad. Today, find one thing in your life that came from far away and has been yours a long time, a recipe, a habit, a song, and give it a moment of thanks. Day one thousand thirty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs in Malaysia and Singapore keep long-established gurdwaras with daily kirtan, langar and Punjabi classes, and families mark gurpurabs and Vaisakhi there as Sikhs do elsewhere.
